youtube.baslik: Planning a Vestibular Rehab Program and Tracking Progress | Lesson 260 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Vestibular rehabilitation works best with a good baseline assessment, measurable goals and regular follow-up. In this lesson we cover the baseline assessment, outcome measures such as the DHI, ABC, DGI and TUG, the home exercise program and progression variables, symptom monitoring, discharge criteria and what to do when progress is poor.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Hall et al., Vestibular rehabilitation for peripheral vestibular hypofunction: an updated clinical practice guideline from the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association, Journal of Neurologic Physical Therapy (2022); Herdman and Clendaniel, Vestibular Rehabilitation; Jacobson and Newman, The development of the Dizziness Handicap Inventory, Archives of Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery (1990); Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Assessment, home program and outcome measurement
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how a vestibular rehabilitation program is planned, how home exercises progress and how outcome is measured.
The content is for education; every program is the individual plan of the qualified clinician who assessed the person.
Planning starts with knowing the cause and duration of dizziness; the approach differs in the acute, subacute and chronic phases.

cumleler.yazi: The 2022 physical therapy guideline counts the first two weeks as acute, up to three months as subacute, and longer as chronic.
cumleler.ses: The twenty twenty two physical therapy guideline counts the first two weeks as acute, up to three months as subacute, and longer as chronic.

cumleler: The video head impulse test, or vHIT, caloric testing and vestibular evoked myogenic potentials, or VEMP, show the site and degree of loss.
Self-report scales put a number on how much daily life is affected and how confident the person is in their balance.
Performance tests measure vision during head movement, standing balance and walking.
Which movements and settings trigger symptoms is also recorded separately.
With this information, measurable goals are set together with the person.
The Dizziness Handicap Inventory, or DHI, is scored from zero to one hundred; a higher score shows greater impact.
The Activities-specific Balance Confidence scale, or ABC, is scored as a percentage; here a higher score shows a better state.
In the dynamic visual acuity test, the number of lines lost during head movement is a functional marker of gaze stabilization.
The Timed Up and Go test, or TUG, shows mobility and fall risk in seconds.
The Dynamic Gait Index, or DGI, assesses balance while walking with eight tasks and a maximum of twenty four points.
The modified Clinical Test of Sensory Interaction and Balance compares standing with eyes open and closed, on firm and soft surfaces.
We saw most of these measures in earlier lessons; here the aim is to track baseline and change with the same measures.
Measures are chosen according to the person's complaint and the program's goals.

maddeler.metin: Step by step, with interim goals

cumleler: A good goal comes from the person's own priorities; for example, being able to shop at the supermarket or return to work.
A goal should be measurable; for example, a meaningful drop in the Dizziness Handicap Inventory score or a shorter walking time.
Each goal has a time frame; for example, within six weeks.
Goals should cover not only test scores but daily activities and participation in social life.
Large goals are broken into small interim goals that can be tracked weekly.
Writing goals together with the person increases adherence and motivation.
The home exercise program is made up of exercises chosen according to the problems found in assessment.
Each exercise is done with the person in the clinic; the right speed, the right target and a safe stance are shown.
The duration, daily repetitions and way to progress each exercise are given in writing or on video.
The person records in a diary whether they did the exercises and how severe their symptoms were.
The guideline notes that a home program can run with weekly clinic visits, and strongly recommends supervised rehabilitation.
At each visit, the program is updated according to the person's progress.
The first way to progress an exercise is to increase the speed of head movement.
The duration of the exercise and the number of daily repetitions are also increased gradually.
Visual difficulty is raised by changing the background from a plain wall to a patterned or moving image.
Posture progresses from sitting to standing, and from there to walking.
The surface changes from firm to soft, and the base of support from wide to narrow.
In the final stage, a second task such as counting or talking while walking is added.
Making only one variable harder at a time makes it easier to understand why symptoms change.
A practical way to monitor symptoms during exercise is to use a symptom score from zero to ten.
In this example, the score is two before exercise and rises to five during it.
After the exercise ends, the score soon falls back to baseline; this shows a suitable intensity.
If the score rises very high and stays up for a long time, the intensity of the exercise is reduced.
Symptoms have been reported to rise temporarily in the first weeks of a program; this alone is no reason to stop.
However, a new symptom, a fall or a decline in general condition is reported to the clinician right away.
This graph shows Dizziness Handicap Inventory scores for an example person with unilateral loss over a six-week program.
The score starts at sixty, drops to fifty four in week two and to thirty four in week six.
The small change in the first weeks may fall within measurement error; so no decision is made from a single interim measurement.
In the Dizziness Handicap Inventory lesson, we saw that a meaningful change requires a difference of about eighteen points.
In this example, the drop of twenty six points is clearly above this threshold.
Over the same period, performance measures such as the Dynamic Gait Index and dynamic visual acuity are repeated under the same conditions.
Improvement on both self-report and performance measures together is the most reliable sign of progress.
According to the guideline, reaching the main goals is a reason to end the program.
Resolution of symptoms, with exercises no longer causing symptoms, is also among the discharge criteria.
Return of balance measures and vestibular function to normal is another criterion.
If measurements show no further progress despite regular work, that is, a plateau, the program can be ended.
The decision weighs both objective measurements and the person's own report.
At the end of the program, a short maintenance program and, if needed, a way to return are given to keep the gains.
If progress is slower than expected, the first question is whether the exercises are really being done, and done correctly.
A new benign paroxysmal positional vertigo may have developed during the program; positional tests are repeated.
Coexisting conditions such as anxiety, depression and migraine can worsen rehabilitation outcomes; referral is made if needed.
Long-term suppressant drug use and visual problems are also reviewed.
With chronic and worsening symptoms, keep in mind a possible shift to persistent postural-perceptual dizziness.
In this case, the approach needs to change and the person should be referred for medical evaluation.
As an example, consider a person two months after left vestibular neuritis with imbalance and blurred vision when turning the head.
At baseline, the Dizziness Handicap Inventory is sixty and the Dynamic Gait Index seventeen points.
The program includes gaze stabilization, balance and walking with head turns.
The person comes to weekly visits and logs the home program in a diary.
In week six, the inventory score drops to thirty four and the gait index rises to twenty two.
As most goals have been reached, the program ends with a maintenance plan; this example is for education only.
Diagnosis of the cause of dizziness and medication decisions belong to the physician.
The audiologist documents baseline status and change with vestibular and hearing tests.
The exercise program is run by a clinician skilled in vestibular rehabilitation, often a physical therapist.
If there is marked anxiety or depression, psychological support is an important part alongside the program.
When team members use the same measures, progress can be tracked in a shared language.

sahneler.metin: Repeat measures under the same conditions each time: same scale, same setting, similar time of day. Showing change on a graph boosts motivation.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: take follow-up measures with the same scale, in the same setting and, if possible, at a similar time of day.
Have self-report scales filled in before testing; fatigue after testing can affect the answers.
Showing the person the change in scores on a simple graph makes progress concrete and boosts motivation.
If the change is within measurement error, say so clearly; keeping expectations realistic protects adherence.
The program starts with knowing the cause and phase, vestibular tests, and self-report and performance measures.
Goals are set from the person's daily life, are measurable and fit within a time frame.
The home exercise program is given in writing, progressed with weekly visits and monitored with a symptom score.
Reaching the goals, resolution of symptoms, return of function to normal or a plateau in progress are reasons for discharge.

sahneler.soru: Which of these is not a discharge criterion in the guideline?
sahneler.aciklama: A _temporary symptom rise_ in the first weeks is no reason to stop on its own.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: which of the following is not a criterion for ending rehabilitation?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: a rise in symptoms in the first week.
Symptoms may rise temporarily at the start of a program; most people improve as they continue.
